---
title: "Genomic Selection"
editor: 
  markdown: 
    wrap: 72
---

If complex traits in livestock are governed by thousands of genes of
small effect, and almost none of them clear the significance threshold
used by MAS, then there is no realistic way to capture the genetic
variance one QTL at a time. Thus, it is recommended to estimate an
effect for every marker in the SNP panel.

Genomic Selection (GS) follows from that one shift. We estimate every
SNP effect simultaneously and skip significance testing. If roughly
10,000 genes affect a trait, those genes are spread across the genome
and will be tagged by many thousands of SNPs. The assumption that every
SNP carries some effect is therefore approximately correct. The
statistical question changes from "which markers are significant?" to
"what is the effect at each marker?".

## The three breakthroughs

There are three breakthroughs that turned the GS idea into operational
practice:

::: {.callout-tip title="The three breakthroughs"}
1.  **The GS methodology itself**: the statistical proposal that all
    marker effects could be estimated simultaneously by treating them as
    random effects drawn from a known distribution (Meuwissen, Hayes &
    Goddard, 2001).
2.  **Massive SNP discovery**: second-generation sequencing of livestock
    genomes uncovered millions of SNPs. In cattle, the 1,000-bulls
    sequencing project alone revealed more than 30 million SNP markers
    (Daetwyler et al., 2014).
3.  **Cost-effective high-throughput genotyping**: SNP-chip platforms
    from Illumina and Affymetrix, with first-generation chips typically
    carry about 50,000 SNPs for each major livestock species.
:::

The methodology was already in print in 2001, but it sat unused in
practice until the second and third pieces caught up. Without millions
of SNPs to choose from, there is nothing to tile a chip with, and
without a cheap chip there is no way to genotype the numbers of animals
that GS needs.

## The statistical model

Assuming a 50,000 SNP panel, the regression model is:

$$
y_i \;=\; \mu \;+\; X_{1i}\,b_1 \;+\; X_{2i}\,b_2 \;+\; \cdots \;+\; X_{50000,\,i}\,b_{50000} \;+\; e_i
$$ {#eq-snp-blup}

where $y_i$ is the phenotype of animal $i$, $\mu$ is the overall mean,
$X_{ki}$ is the genotype of animal $i$ at SNP $k$, $b_k$ is the effect
of SNP $k$, and $e_i$ is the residual.

A reference population of less than 50,000 animals cannot estimate
50,000 fixed SNP effects, so GS treats the SNP effects as random draws
from a known distribution. This is a Bayesian framework in which the
prior on the effects is what makes the system identifiable. The default
prior is normally distributed effects with mean zero and a constant
variance equal to the total genetic variance divided by the number of
SNPs.

Once the effects have been estimated on the reference population, the
genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV) for a selection candidate $j$ is
simply the inner product of the candidate's genotype vector with the
estimated effects:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{GEBV}}_j \;=\; X_{1j}\,\hat{b}_1 \;+\; X_{2j}\,\hat{b}_2 \;+\; \cdots \;+\; X_{50000,\,j}\,\hat{b}_{50000}.
$$

## Why this is a paradigm shift, not an incremental upgrade

There are two structural changes that follow from the GS workflow:

-   **Pedigree becomes optional.** Traditional BLUP-EBV requires
    pedigree recording. SNP-BLUP requires the SNP genotypes of the
    animals in the reference population and the candidates, but not the
    pedigree of either.
-   **Elite breeding animals no longer need to be trait-recorded.**
    Under traditional BLUP, the selection candidates were the animals
    most carefully phenotyped, because their own records (or records of
    their progeny) drove their EBVs. Under GS, accurate phenotypes are
    needed only on the reference population. The selection candidates
    can be genotyped and ranked without ever carrying records.

The GS approach has the *potential* to decouple accurate recording from
the elite breeding population, which makes it possible to redesign the
breeding scheme from the ground up. Whether a given national or
commercial scheme actually exercises that potential is a separate
operational question. Breeders gather phenotypes wherever they are
easiest to obtain, like commercial herds, progeny-tested historical
bulls, slaughter lines, and then base selection decisions on genotyped
young candidates that no one has measured.
